barzakh.name: Barzakh
barzakh.card: **Al-Barzakh** (the Isthmus). In Ibn Turka's system, the intermediate realm between pure matter and pure spirit, between multiplicity and unity. The domain where letters become forms, where Divine Names manifest as causal powers, where mathematics governs physical existence. Central to understanding how lettrism operates—letters do not merely represent reality but constitute the barzakh through which divine principles become concrete.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 150-180.

imaginal-realm.name: The Imaginal Realm
imaginal-realm.card: **Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (The Imaginal Realm). In Ibn Arabi's metaphysics, the ontological layer between pure intellect and material sense where forms (*ashkāl*) exist independently of physical matter. The domain where mystical visions occur, where symbols manifest, where divine names express themselves in subtle forms. Central to understanding how knowledge operates in Islamic mysticism and occultism: the imaginal realm is where letters and divine names acquire form, where talismanic operations work, where the barzakh functions.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Imaginal Ontology and the New Brethren of Purity*.

suhrawardi.name: Suhrawardi
suhrawardi.card: **Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi** (1154–1191). Founder of Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) philosophy. Synthesized Neoplatonic emanationism with Islamic theology, emphasizing direct mystical intuition (*ishraq*; illumination) of divine light and angelic powers. Executed in Aleppo for his teachings. His system profoundly influenced later Islamic philosophers and occultists, including Ibn Turka, who adopted Illuminationist vocabulary and framework to ground lettrist doctrine.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 50-80.

oneiromancy.name: Oneiromancy (ʿilm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā)
oneiromancy.card: **ʿIlm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā** — the science of dream interpretation, and the occult science this portal has most consistently underrated. Melvin-Koushki ranks it **second in popularity only to astrology** across the early modern Islamicate world, ahead of geomancy and lettrism alike. Its classificatory definition is unusually precise: physiognomy inquires into the inner states of rational souls **while they are conscious**, and oneiromancy does the same **while they are unconscious**. Both are readings of a soul; only the soul's condition differs.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *In Defense of Geomancy*, 6; *Geomancy in the Islamic World*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, *Divining Past, Present, and Future in the Sand*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science*, 58 n.16.

pythagorean-cosmology.name: Pythagorean Cosmology
pythagorean-cosmology.card: **Pythagorean Cosmology**. The ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles governing reality. Ibn Turka's distinctive contribution was grounding Islamic lettrism explicitly in Pythagorean mathematics, arguing that letters and their numerical values encode cosmic principles just as Pythagoras taught that mathematics is the language of creation. This synthesis gave Islamic lettrism mathematical legitimacy and positioned it as a **truly universal science** encompassing reason, mysticism, and operative power.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.

neoplatonism.name: Neoplatonism
neoplatonism.card: **Neoplatonism**. The late-antique emanationist philosophy of Plotinus and Proclus, which reached Islamdom in Arabic translation and was never, in Melvin-Koushki's usage, quite separable from its Pythagorean twin — he writes of *neopythagorean-neoplatonic* philosophy as one tradition. Ibn Turka's contribution was not to receive it but to **reclassify** it: he treated this philosophy as prophetically revealed rather than merely Greek, and made its mathematics the ground on which the occult sciences could be defended as sciences at all.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: The Mathematicalization of the Occult Sciences in the High Persianate Tradition*, 1, 127–28.

sufism.name: Sufism
sufism.card: **Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism). Islamic mysticism emphasizing direct experiential knowledge of the divine through discipline, contemplation, and often ecstatic experience. Developed systematically from 9th century onward; by Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was integral to Islamic orthodoxy. Ibn Arabi, Suhrawardi, Al-Ghazali, and other philosophical predecessors were Sufi-philosophers. Ibn Turka inherited and operationalized Sufi gnosis through lettrism, positioning occult science as Sufi practice systematized into rational discipline.
literature: Chittick, William C. The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination.

geomancy.name: Geomancy (ʿilm al-raml)
geomancy.card: **ʿIlm al-raml**, the science of sand — divination by generating figures from marks made at random and reading them through a fixed combinatorial system. One of the three sciences Melvin-Koushki tracks as shifting **from the natural to the mathematical** in this period, alongside astrology and lettrism. It is also the ground of the portal's sharpest confrontation: **Ibn Khaldūn against Yazdī** — which does not run the way the reputations suggest.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Divining Past, Present, and Future in the Sand*, 1, 9.

jafr.name: Jafr
jafr.card: **Jafr** — letter divination, and the political edge of lettrism. Its inventor is held to be **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib**, who in this tradition is hailed **the chief mathematician of Islam**; its foundational text is the *K. al-Jafr wa-l-Jāmiʿa*, an omniscient book recording past and future history and all knowledge of the cosmos. The dissertation gives it a chapter, under the heading **political uses of lettrism**.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 22, 41, ch. 5.

sayyid-husayn-akhlati.name: Akhlati
sayyid-husayn-akhlati.card: **Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī** (d. 1397), Kurdish occultist, alchemist, and lettrist mystic. The pivot of the "New Brethren of Purity" network stretching from Cairo through Anatolia to Iran, Central Asia, and India. Served as physician and confidant at the court of Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 1382–1399). Akhlāṭī's oral teachings on lettrism, alchemy, and talismanic magic shaped Ibn Turka, who became his principal systematizer and heir. Though Akhlāṭī left few written works, his influence on Islamic occultism proved foundational and lasting.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran.* PhD Dissertation, Yale University, 2012. [See especially Chapter 1 on Akhlāṭī and the Cairo Circle.]
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'The New Brethren of Purity: Intellectual Lettrist Networks in the Fifteenth-Century Islamic World.' *Journal of the American Oriental Society* 139, no. 3 (2019): 541–572.

cairo-bustan.why: The isthmus between spirit and body: the reading Yūsuf Ascent applies to the impossible stair in f. 52b.
The ontological layer where forms subsist as images — the realm the 'diagram, not building' reading places Bihzād's palace in.

miraj.why: Illuminationist philosophy makes ascent through light the philosopher's path — the doctrinal frame in which miʿrāj painting was read.
The domain where mystical visions occur: where an ascent narrative locates what its images depict.

Dream divination ranked second only to astrology across this world — ahead of geomancy and lettrism. An ascension cycle is the prestige case of the thing it reads: cognition continuing while the body is unconscious.

haft-paykar.why: Number, harmony and the seven planets as cosmic order — the correspondence table Nizami's seven pavilions are built on.
Emanation through the planetary spheres: the cosmological ladder Bahrām Gūr's colour-by-colour progress enacts.

siyah-qalam.why: The unresolved scholarly debate over these paintings is precisely whether the figures are Sufis or demons.
Beings painted with no ground under them — the closest visual analogue in the corpus to forms subsisting without material substrate.

ajaib.why: Qazwīnī's cosmography orders creation as a descending hierarchy from angels to minerals — the emanationist frame made into an index.

falnama.why: The divinatory science standing behind Islamicate omen-books. Ibn Turka's closest associate Yazdī wrote its defense against Ibn Khaldūn, so divination sits inside this circle's metaphysics rather than beside it. The Falnāma is bibliomancy on pictures and a century later: a link of kind, not lineage.
Letter divination — the political edge of lettrism, and the nearest thing in the portal to reading a fixed image for what it discloses.

jalayirid.why: The occultist network Akhlāṭī pivoted — Cairo through Anatolia to Iran — spans exactly the courts and decades these drawings come from.
The standard reading of the Dīwān's marginal drawings: the soul's quest, evoked rather than illustrated.

mantiq.why: ʿAṭṭār's epic is the Sufi path itself: thirty birds seeking the Simurgh and finding themselves.
